knowledge-base.overview: Language-specific idioms, guardrails, and patterns for Ruby 3.2+. Loaded automatically when agents work on .rb, .rake, or .gemspec files. Applies to gems, web applications, APIs, and CLIs. Covers frozen string literals, blocks/procs, metaprogramming guardrails, modern pattern matching, enumerable idioms, and testing with RSpec and FactoryBot.

core-principles.principle: Code should behave as readers expect. Prefer clarity over cleverness.
Leverage Ruby's object model. Primitives are objects with methods.
Follow established naming and structure conventions.
Rely on behavior, not class checks. Validate at system boundaries.
Use blocks for resource management, iteration, and DSLs.

guardrail.rule: Every `.rb` file must start with `# frozen_string_literal: true`. This prevents accidental string mutation and improves performance. Use `+""` or `.dup` when mutable strings are genuinely required.
guardrail.bad: # Missing frozen_string_literal comment class UserService NAME = "service" end
guardrail.good:
# frozen_string_literal: true
class UserService NAME = "service" MUTABLE = +"mutable string" # intentionally mutable end

guardrail.rule: Never use bare `rescue` (rescues all exceptions including system errors). Always rescue specific exception classes.
guardrail.bad: def charge(account, amount) account.debit(amount) rescue # catches SignalException, NoMemoryError, etc. nil end
guardrail.good: def charge(account, amount) account.debit(amount) rescue InsufficientFundsError => e raise PaymentError, "card declined: #{e.message}" rescue Stripe::CardError => e logger.error("Stripe error for account=#{account.id}: #{e.message}") raise PaymentError, "payment gateway error" end

guardrail.rule: Never use `eval` with string arguments. Use the block form of `class_eval` or `module_eval` when dynamic method definition is unavoidable.
Always pair `method_missing` with `respond_to_missing?`. Without it, `respond_to?` and other reflection methods return incorrect results.
guardrail.bad: def method_missing(name, *args) find_by_attribute(name.to_s, args.first) if name.to_s.start_with?("find_by_") end # respond_to_missing? not defined — breaks respond_to?, method(), etc.

guardrail.rule: Run `bundle audit` before merging. Commit `Gemfile.lock` for applications; omit for gems. Never use `gem "name"` without a version constraint in production code.
guardrail.bad: gem "rails" # no version — gets whatever is latest
guardrail.good: gem "rails", "~> 7.1" # pessimistic constraint — allows patch/minor up to 8.0

guardrail.rule: Run `rubocop` before every commit. Zero offenses required in CI. Use `bundle exec rubocop -a` to auto-fix safe cops.
Prefer guard clauses over nested conditionals. A method that returns early is easier to read than deeply nested branches.
guardrail.bad: def process(user) if user if user.active? do_something(user) if user.verified? end end end
guardrail.good:
def process(user) return unless user return unless user.active? return unless user.verified?
do_something(user) end

guardrail.rule: Use `define_method` sparingly. Prefer explicit method definitions for readability and static analysis. Never use metaprogramming in hot paths.
Prefer `Module#prepend` over `alias_method` chains. `prepend` inserts the module before the class in the inheritance chain and is easier to follow.
Validate duck-typed inputs at system boundaries (public methods, service entry points). Use `respond_to?` or Sorbet/RBS type signatures. Fail fast with a descriptive `TypeError` or `ArgumentError`.
guardrail.good: def serialize(obj) raise TypeError, "expected #to_h, got #{obj.class}" unless obj.respond_to?(:to_h) obj.to_h end

guardrail.rule: Use `{}` for single-line blocks, `do...end` for multi-line. Prefer `block_given?` + `yield` over explicit `&block` parameter unless the proc must be stored.
guardrail.good: def each items.each { |i| yield i } if block_given? end

guardrail.rule: Use lambdas (`->`) for strict arity checking and when the proc should return from itself. Use procs only for flexible arity or block-like behavior.
Use `ensure` for cleanup (file handles, connections). Never use `rescue` for control flow — it is for exception handling.
guardrail.bad: def read_file(path) f = File.open(path) f.read rescue f&.close # wrong — rescue is not a finally block end
guardrail.good: def read_file(path) File.open(path) { |f| f.read } # or with explicit ensure: # f = File.open(path) # f.read # ensure # f&.close end

guardrail.rule: Custom errors must inherit from `StandardError` (not `Exception`). Provide a `#message` with actionable information. Define an error hierarchy per domain.
guardrail.good: class PaymentError < StandardError; end class InsufficientFundsError < PaymentError; end

project-structure.description: Gem and application layouts following Ruby conventions.
project-structure.gem-layout: mygem/ ├── lib/ │ ├── mygem.rb # Entry point, require dependencies │ └── mygem/ │ ├── version.rb # VERSION constant │ ├── client.rb # Core logic │ └── errors.rb # Custom error classes ├── spec/ │ ├── spec_helper.rb │ └── mygem/ │ └── client_spec.rb ├── Gemfile ├── mygem.gemspec └── Rakefile
project-structure.application-layout: myapp/ ├── app/ │ ├── models/ # Domain objects │ ├── services/ # Business logic (POROs) │ └── validators/ # Input validation ├── config/ ├── db/migrate/ # Database migrations ├── lib/tasks/ # Rake tasks ├── spec/ │ ├── spec_helper.rb │ ├── models/ │ └── services/ ├── Gemfile ├── Gemfile.lock └── Rakefile

rules.rule: Service objects for business logic — single public method `#call`
One class per file; file name matches class name in snake_case
No global mutable state; use dependency injection or configuration objects

pattern.name: Guard clauses
pattern.context: Any method with conditional early returns
pattern.example:
# frozen_string_literal: true
def process(user) return unless user return unless user.active? return unless user.verified?
do_something(user) end

pattern.name: Enumerable and lazy evaluation
pattern.context: Collection transformations — prefer over imperative loops
pattern.example:
# Chain Enumerable methods over manual loops users.select(&:active?).map(&:email).sort
# Lazy evaluation for large or infinite collections File.open("huge.log").each_line.lazy .select { |line| line.include?("ERROR") } .map { |line| parse_error(line) } .first(10)
# each_with_object for building hashes totals = orders.each_with_object(Hash.new(0)) do |order, sums| sums[order.category] += order.amount end
# Point-free style with Symbol#to_proc names = users.map(&:name)

pattern.name: Pattern matching (Ruby 3.x)
pattern.context: Destructuring hashes, arrays, and API responses
pattern.example:
case response in { status: 200, body: { data: Array => items } } process_items(items) in { status: 404 } handle_not_found in { status: (500..) } handle_server_error end
# Pin operator for variable binding expected_id = 42 case record in { id: ^expected_id, name: String => name } puts "Found: #{name}" end

pattern.name: Frozen string literals and immutability
pattern.example:
# frozen_string_literal: true
name = "hello" # name << " world" # => FrozenError in Ruby 3.x
# Use +'' or .dup when mutation is needed mutable = +"hello" mutable << " world" # => "hello world"
VALID_STATUSES = %w[pending active suspended].freeze CONFIG_DEFAULTS = { timeout: 30, retries: 3 }.freeze

pattern.name: Custom errors with hierarchy
pattern.context: Domain services — define before writing business logic
pattern.example:
# frozen_string_literal: true
class PaymentError < StandardError; end class InsufficientFundsError < PaymentError; end
def charge(account, amount) raise InsufficientFundsError, "account #{account.id} needs #{amount}" if account.balance < amount
account.debit(amount) rescue Stripe::CardError => e Rails.logger.error("Payment failed for account=#{account.id}: #{e.message}") raise PaymentError, "card declined: #{e.message}" end

pattern.name: Metaprogramming with method_missing
pattern.context: Only when explicit methods are impractical — always pair with respond_to_missing?
pattern.example:
# frozen_string_literal: true
class DynamicFinder def method_missing(method_name, *args) if method_name.to_s.start_with?("find_by_") attribute = method_name.to_s.delete_prefix("find_by_") find_by_attribute(attribute, args.first) else super end end
def respond_to_missing?(method_name, include_private = false) method_name.to_s.start_with?("find_by_") || super end
private
def find_by_attribute(attribute, value) collection.find { |item| item.public_send(attribute) == value } end end

pattern.name: Ractor for true parallelism (Ruby 3.x)
pattern.context: CPU-bound parallel work — only with Ractor-safe (shareable) objects
pattern.example:
workers = 4.times.map do Ractor.new do loop do task = Ractor.receive Ractor.yield expensive_computation(task) end end end
tasks.each_with_index { |task, i| workers[i % workers.size].send(task) } results = workers.map(&:take)

rules.rule: `describe` for class/method; `context` for scenario (prefix with "when" or "with")
`let` for lazy data; `let!` only when eager evaluation is required
`subject` for the object under test; `described_class` over hardcoded class names
Prefer `instance_double` over generic `double` for type safety
Use shared examples for behavior shared across classes
Use `webmock` or `vcr` for HTTP stubbing — no real network in unit tests
All bug fixes include a regression test
Test edge cases: nil, empty string, empty array, boundary values

rubocop-config.example: # .rubocop.yml require: - rubocop-rspec - rubocop-performance AllCops: NewCops: enable TargetRubyVersion: 3.2 Style/FrozenStringLiteralComment: Enabled: true EnforcedStyle: always Metrics/MethodLength: Max: 20 Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity: Max: 10

bundler-gemfile.description: Gemfile template with pinned versions and group separation.
bundler-gemfile.example:
# Gemfile source "https://rubygems.org" ruby "~> 3.2"
gem "dry-struct", "~> 1.6" gem "zeitwerk", "~> 2.6"
group :development, :test do gem "rspec", "~> 3.13" gem "rubocop", "~> 1.60", require: false gem "factory_bot", "~> 6.4" end
group :test do gem "simplecov", require: false gem "webmock", "~> 3.19" end

quick-reference.item: # frozen_string_literal: true at top of every .rb file
Always rescue specific exceptions — never bare rescue
String eval is banned — use define_method or block form of class_eval
Must always be paired with respond_to_missing?
Prefer over nested conditionals — return early
{ } for single-line, do...end for multi-line; yield over &block when not stored
Lambda: strict arity, returns from lambda; Proc: flexible, returns from enclosing method
Chain select/map/reduce over manual loops; lazy for large collections
Use case/in with Ruby 3.x for hash/array destructuring
Inherit from StandardError; hierarchy per domain; ensure for cleanup
Sparingly; never in hot paths; always document why
Zero offenses required in CI; run before every commit
Pessimistic version constraints (~>); bundle audit in CI
80% business logic minimum, 60% overall with simplecov
Prefer over generic double for type-safe mocks in RSpec
